subject: iceCreamCart
pitch: A cheerful seaside ice cream cart. A mint and cream body with a scalloped striped canopy in pink and white, two big spoked wheels, a push handle, a chrome lid over the freezer, a hand-painted sign shaped like a cone, and a row of giant fake ice cream cones in pastel flavours along the top.
reasoning:
Since this is scenery rather than a creature, I can use plain objects without joints, though I'll keep a root joint for structure since parts require a bone. I'll stick to the most reliable SDK calls—createBuilder, joints, parts, sweeps, lathes, and extrusions—to keep the module correct and runnable as-is.

Now I'm planning the cart's dimensions: roughly 1.6m long, 2.2m tall with canopy, 0.9m wide, facing +Z. I'm working out wheel placement using torus geometry rotated to align its axis along X, spokes as thin boxes, and cylindrical hubs aimed along the X direction using the dir parameter.

I'm sketching the body as a mint-colored box sitting above the wheel axles, then adding a chrome freezer lid on top using a flattened box or sphere to suggest a rounded hump.

For the canopy, I'm thinking through how to build a scalloped pink-and-white striped awning that arcs forward over the cart, considering a vaulted sweep shape stretching from back to front supported by corner poles.

This is getting complicated—maybe I should try a lathe approach or a sweep whose path arcs over the top width-wise, like a semicircle spanning the X-axis at the top.

Actually a cleaner trick: use a half cylinder geometry oriented so its arc lies in the XY plane rather than XZ, achieved by rotating the default cylinder geometry about the Z axis so the semicircular cap faces upward.

That confirms the top half arc configuration. I'll set the canopy radius around 0.62 for a slight overhang beyond the 0.9-wide cart, giving a cheerful awning look, with the arch apex reaching about 2.07 when mounted at y=1.45.

For texturing, I'm using UV coordinates on the cylinder geometry to create lengthwise stripes, alternating pink and cream based on the u-coordinate going around the arc, which gives the classic awning pattern. I'm also planning a scalloped valance along the front edge using a row of rounded bumps.

Positioning scallops as flattened spheres along the arc, slightly lower than the edge, alternating pink and white. Now adding chrome support poles running from the body corners up to the canopy.

Switching to wheels now, checking that radius and axle placement don't cause unwanted overlap with the body sides.

For spokes, I'm planning six thin rotated boxes radiating from the hub, oriented in the YZ plane so they sit flush against the wheel face, with a chrome cylindrical hub capping the center.

The wheel rims use torus geometry rotated to lie in the X-axis plane, positioned symmetrically on either side of the cart body. For the push handle at the back, I'm sketching a U-shaped chrome bar using a swept catmull-rom path that angles upward and backward from the body, then sizing the main mint-colored body box to fit the overall cart proportions.

I'm now adding a cream freezer lid as a squashed dome sitting half-buried into the top-front of the body, and considering a cone-shaped hand-painted sign mounted on a pole near the front-top corner to give that classic ice cream cart look.

I'm checking whether the sign placement conflicts with the awning geometry — if positioned at the current height it ends up hidden inside the arch shell, visible only from the front opening, so I need to reposition it lower and in front of the body instead, away from the freezer area.

Now for the ice cream cones in pastel flavors — I'm thinking of placing them in a row along the top of the body, maybe on a small rail near the back since the freezer lid occupies the front.

Writing cone geometry code...

I'll embed the cone tips slightly into the body top so the base sits higher, with scoop spheres positioned just above the cone bases to complete the ice-cream silhouette.

Now I'm realizing the freezer lid and the cone row risk overlapping in the z-axis, so I'm shifting the lid forward and spacing four cones along the back with enough gap between scoops to avoid collisions.

I'm settling on two staggered rows of three cones at x=±0.2, keeping clear of the lid's footprint, and moving on to pick pastel flavor colors for the scoops.

For the cones themselves I'll use a plain waffle-tan color rather than a textured grain paint, since that could look too busy at this scale. For the awning stripes, I'm planning a custom UV-based paint function that alternates pink and cream bands along the length, importing the paint helper from the SDK.

Checking the cylinder's UV mapping, I confirm the circumferential coordinate works well for driving the stripe pattern across the half-arc of the awning. I'm also considering whether the open underside of the shell will show visible backfaces from below, but since the awning is mainly viewed from outside and the scalloped valance covers the front edge, this shouldn't be a real issue.

I'm working through the rotation math to confirm the cylinder arch sits correctly in the XY plane with its axis along Z after rotating 90 degrees around X, verifying that the top of the arc lands at the expected height and the translated position places the canopy correctly relative to the body.

Now I'm positioning the scalloped valance along the front edge of the awning arc, parameterizing points along the curve and placing small flattened spheres that hang just below each point, alternating pink and cream colors to match the striped pattern.

I'm then working through where to anchor the canopy support poles — trying to figure out whether they should attach at the body's edge or extend out to meet the shell's arc, since the geometry means the poles and shell don't naturally line up unless I adjust the pole positions or angle them as brackets between the body and the awning's underside.

I decide to lower the canopy's center and reduce its radius, so the poles can connect more cleanly from the body top to the shell's edge without being excessively tall, then recompute the scallop arc points and the canopy's front-to-back extent along z. With that settled, I shift focus to placing the sign — sketching a flat-topped triangular outline positioned a bit above and in front of the body.

Now I'm redesigning the sign as a classic ice cream shape: a waffle-tan triangle cone with a separate pink scoop sphere sitting on top, positioning both so the scoop clears the body top and the sign sits flush against the lid's front face. I'm working out the extrusion axes and outline coordinates so the sign's edges align with the body surface, and considering whether to add a waffle cross-hatch texture using the scales helper.

Then I'm adding a tiny red cherry sphere atop the scoop, and planning a cream trim band around the cart's base to cover the bottom edge of the mint body while leaving clearance for the wheels. I'm also considering adding a front window panel — either cream or tinted blue-glass — to suggest a freezer display, positioned just behind the sign.

I decide to skip the front window and side windows since they overlap the sign area, and focus instead on finalizing the lid as a flattened, scaled sphere nestled into the body. I'm settling on a limited color palette — mint, cream, pink, chrome, waffle-brown, and dark — and assigning them to parts like the torus rims, spokes, and hub, choosing dark rims with cream spokes and chrome hubs for a classic ice-cream-cart look.

I'm setting up a single root joint for the cart with all parts rigidly attached to it, since there's no need for multiple bones or chains in this simple prop. I'm also double-checking wheel placement so the tires' lowest point sits exactly at ground level, calculating axle height from the wheel radius plus tube thickness, and making sure the body sits above the wheels without overlapping them.

Working out vertical positions...

I need to adjust the scallop spheres so they hang below the awning edge rather than straddling it, tweaking their z-scale and offset. For coloring, I'll alternate the scallops between pink and cream, and set up the stripe paint function using the u-coordinate across the awning's circumference to determine the color bands.

Now I'm working through the full construction: cone-and-scoop ice cream toppers with rotated cones and overlapping sphere scoops, a cherry on the sign's scoop, and the wheel assembly with a torus rim, six spoke boxes rotated at 30-degree increments, and a chrome hub cylinder. I'm also laying out the body as a mint box with a pink trim band and cream base skirt, a chrome dome lid, support poles and a swept handle using catmull splines, and a hand-painted sign extruded from an outline with beveled edges—checking that all the colors, scales, and positions (wheels, cones, poles, trim) line up proportionally without clipping into each other, then starting to write the actual builder code with joints, parts, colors, and geometry calls for the cart, awning, scallops, wheels, body, cones, and handle.
